patient.history_present_illness: A 63-year-old man with known hepatitis C cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma on the liver transplant waiting list was brought to the emergency department by his wife due to three days of progressively worsening confusion. His wife reports that he initially seemed forgetful and was mixing up family members' names, which she attributed to fatigue. By day two, he was sleeping most of the day, becoming difficult to rouse for meals, and had stopped taking his afternoon lactulose dose because he kept forgetting. On the day of presentation, he could not recognize their home and was asking to go back to Mexico (he has lived in the United States for 35 years). He had no witnessed seizures, no falls, no headaches, and no complaints of pain. His wife noted his abdomen appeared more distended than usual and that his urine had been darker over the past two days. She also reported that he had developed a low-grade fever at home (measured 38.2°C) and had complained of mild abdominal discomfort. He has been compliant with his transplant evaluation requirements and had a routine hepatology appointment scheduled for next week. He has been abstinent from alcohol for 8 years and achieved sustained virologic response on hepatitis C treatment. His wife denied any recent medication changes, new supplements, or obvious dietary indiscretions. He had a prior episode of hepatic encephalopathy eighteen months ago that required hospitalization but resolved completely with lactulose and rifaximin intensification.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Hepatic encephalopathy, Grade 2-3, precipitated by spontaneous bacterial peritonitis

differential.key_features: Toxicology not obtained initially but patient's medication list includes no CNS depressants; alcohol abstinent 8 years; urine tox negative
Creatinine elevated (1.6) at CKD2 baseline but insufficient to cause encephalopathy at this level; ammonia markedly elevated (142 umol/L) pointing to hepatic cause
Na 131 mEq/L — contributes to encephalopathy but not sufficiently low (<125) to be sole cause; HE is primary
No meningismus, fever is low-grade (38.4), CT normal, SBP confirmed as infection source; LP not indicated
CT head shows no intracranial metastases; HCC rarely metastasizes to brain

optimal_actions.action: Perform CT head to exclude structural cause of encephalopathy
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Normal CT head — no hemorrhage, infarct, or HCC brain metastasis

optimal_actions.action: Order stat labs: ammonia, CBC, CMP, LFTs, coagulation, CRP, procalcitonin, blood cultures
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Ammonia 142 umol/L markedly elevated; elevated inflammatory markers (CRP 48.2, PCT 1.8) suggesting infection; liver dysfunction markers

optimal_actions.action: Perform EEG to characterize encephalopathy and exclude NCSE
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Triphasic waves with generalized slowing — metabolic encephalopathy pattern consistent with HE; no ictal activity

optimal_actions.action: Perform diagnostic paracentesis to exclude SBP (given fever, abdominal symptoms, leukocytosis)
optimal_actions.expected_finding: PMN 380/mm3 — SBP confirmed; Gram-negative rods on Gram stain (E. coli)

optimal_actions.action: Start IV cefotaxime 2g q8h for SBP (patient has sulfa allergy — do NOT use TMP-SMX)
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Antibiotic treatment initiated; SBP precipitant addressed

optimal_actions.action: Administer IV albumin 1.5 g/kg on day 1 to prevent hepatorenal syndrome in SBP
Optimize lactulose (30mL q2h until 2-3 stools/day) and continue rifaximin 550mg BID
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Ammonia trending down; encephalopathy grade improving

optimal_actions.action: Check drug interactions for cefotaxime with current medications given sulfa allergy
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Cefotaxime safe — not a sulfonamide; no significant interactions with current regimen

optimal_actions.expected_finding: MELD 22, MELD-Na 25 — patient remains transplant candidate; SBP may qualify for exception points

optimal_actions.expected_finding: PMN 142/mm3 at 48h — confirmed response; E. coli pansensitive on culture

critical_actions: Perform diagnostic paracentesis to identify SBP as the precipitant
Start IV cefotaxime (NOT sulfa-containing antibiotics — patient has sulfa allergy) for confirmed SBP
Administer IV albumin 1.5 g/kg on day 1 to prevent hepatorenal syndrome
Optimize lactulose and rifaximin for ammonia reduction
Notify transplant team of SBP episode immediately
CT head to exclude structural cause including HCC brain metastasis
Repeat paracentesis at 48 hours to document antibiotic response
After SBP resolution, initiate secondary prophylaxis with norfloxacin (NOT TMP-SMX — sulfa allergy)
contraindicated_actions: Do NOT use trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX) — patient has documented sulfa allergy (anaphylaxis)
Do NOT use benzodiazepines for agitation — worsens hepatic encephalopathy
Do NOT rapidly correct hyponatremia (osmotic demyelination risk)
Do NOT delay paracentesis — SBP is the primary precipitant that must be identified and treated
key_reasoning_points: Fever + abdominal symptoms + leukocytosis + elevated CRP/procalcitonin in a cirrhotic patient mandates diagnostic paracentesis to rule out SBP
SBP (PMN 380/mm3, E. coli) was the primary precipitant for hepatic encephalopathy (ammonia 142 umol/L)
Patient had sulfa allergy (anaphylaxis) — cefotaxime, not TMP-SMX, is the appropriate first-line SBP treatment
IV albumin co-administration with SBP antibiotics reduces hepatorenal syndrome risk by 66%
Known HCC within Milan criteria — transplant team notification is critical; SBP episode is a decompensating event
EEG triphasic waves confirm metabolic (hepatic) encephalopathy and exclude NCSE
After SBP resolution, secondary prophylaxis is mandatory given >70% 1-year recurrence rate
